d.chapter: Economic Geography — Natural Regions: 2. The Tropical Grassland Region
d.notions: Drought, bush fire, overgrazing, soil erosion, desertification, poaching, farmer–herder conflict.
d.focus: Problems faced in the Tropical Grassland region and the solutions attempted.
d.competence: Learners are able to take simple actions against bush fires and soil erosion around their homes.
objectives: Identify the problems faced by people in the Tropical Grassland region.
Explain the causes of these problems.
Describe the solutions attempted to solve them.
recall: The people of the savanna practise crop farming, livestock rearing, hunting and fishing.
Herders move with their animals in the dry season (transhumance).
d.recallNote: Check the homework: problems faced by farmers and herders around Garoua.
situation: In a village near Garoua, a herder's cattle entered a farmer's field at night and ate his maize. The farmer was very angry, and the two men started to fight.
The village chief called them. He wants to find a solution so that this does not happen again.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is a conflict between a farmer and a herder, because the herder's cattle ate the farmer's maize.
Why did the cattle enter the field?
They entered the field to eat, because pasture is scarce and there was no one to guard them at night.
What can the chief do to prevent such conflicts?
He can mark paths for the animals, separate farming zones from grazing zones, and ask herders to guard their cattle.
d.justification: This lesson will help us to understand the problems of the savanna and the solutions people have found, so that we can protect our environment.

qa.q: Some years, the rains start late or stop early. What problem does this cause for farmers?
qa.a: It causes drought. Crops dry up, harvests are poor and there can be famine.

qa.q: In the dry season, bush fires burn large areas of savanna. Give two dangers of bush fires.
qa.a: Bush fires destroy grass, trees and animals, and they leave the soil bare, so it is easily eroded.

qa.q: Too many cattle graze on the same land. What happens to the grass and the soil?
qa.a: The grass disappears and the soil becomes bare. This is called overgrazing. The soil is then washed away by rain or blown by wind.

qa.q: Give two other problems of the savanna: one linked to animals and one linked to people.
qa.a: Locusts and the tsetse fly harm crops and cattle. Poachers kill protected animals, and farmers and herders sometimes fight.

sum.title: I. Problems Faced
sum.intro: The main problems faced in the Tropical Grassland region are the following:
items: A. Irregular Rainfall and Drought
The rains sometimes start late or stop early. Crops dry up, harvests are poor and famine can follow.
B. Bush Fires
Bush fires destroy grass, trees and animals. They leave the soil bare and easy to erode.
C. Overgrazing and Soil Erosion
Too many animals eat all the grass. The bare soil is washed away by rain or blown away by wind.
D. Desertification
In the drier savanna, the land slowly turns into desert because of drought, overgrazing and the cutting of trees.
E. Pests and Diseases
Locusts and birds destroy crops. The tsetse fly carries sleeping sickness in cattle and people.
F. Poaching and Conflicts
Poachers kill protected animals. Farmers and herders fight over land and water.

qa.q: How can farmers still grow crops when the rains are irregular?
qa.a: They can irrigate their fields with water from dams and wells, and grow crops that resist drought, such as millet and sorghum.

qa.q: What is the name of the Cameroonian programme that plants trees to stop the desert in the North?
qa.a: It is called Opération Sahel Vert. Across Africa, the Great Green Wall project also plants trees in the Sahel.

qa.q: How can the government protect wild animals from poachers?
qa.a: It creates national parks, trains and arms eco-guards, and punishes poachers.

sum.title: II. Attempted Solutions
sum.intro: The main solutions attempted in the Tropical Grassland region are the following:
items: A. Irrigation and Drought-Resistant Crops
Dams and wells supply water to fields. Farmers grow millet and sorghum, which resist drought.
B. Reforestation
Trees are planted to stop desertification, as in Opération Sahel Vert in Cameroon and the Great Green Wall in the Sahel.
C. Fire Control
Early controlled burning, firebreaks and education reduce the damage caused by bush fires.
D. Better Management of Land
Grazing zones and cattle paths are marked, and fodder is stored. Crop rotation and manure keep the soil fertile.
E. Protection of Wildlife and Pest Control
National parks and eco-guards protect animals. Insecticides and vaccination fight pests and diseases.

evaluation: Explain how overgrazing leads to soil erosion.
Too many animals eat all the grass. The bare soil is then washed away by rain or blown away by wind.
Give two solutions to the problem of drought.
Farmers can irrigate their fields and grow drought-resistant crops such as millet and sorghum.
Give one cause of conflicts between farmers and herders.
Cattle enter fields and eat crops, because pasture and water are scarce.
remediation: A long period without enough rain is called a ______.
Too many animals grazing on the same land is called ______.
The fly that carries sleeping sickness is the ______ fly.
The illegal killing of protected animals is called ______.
The Cameroonian tree-planting programme in the North is called Opération ______.
Burning small areas early in the dry season is called ______ burning.
d.remediationAnswers: 1. drought 2. overgrazing 3. tsetse 4. poaching 5. Sahel Vert 6. controlled (early)
